lesson.title: So, What Is Computer Science, Really?
lesson.summary: Introduces computer science as the study of computation, problems, and the algorithms and abstractions used to solve them, not merely the act of typing code.
lesson.body:
Many people hear "computer science" and picture someone typing code into a laptop, but that image only shows the surface. Computer science is the study of computation itself: what problems can be solved by following a precise set of instructions, how to describe those instructions clearly, and how to carry them out efficiently. A chef follows a recipe, a musician follows sheet music, and a computer follows a program. Computer science is the discipline that studies how to write those "recipes" so that a machine, which understands nothing on its own, can still produce useful results.

It helps to separate computer science from two things it is often confused with: computer literacy and programming. Computer literacy means knowing how to use existing software, such as sending an email or opening a spreadsheet. Programming is the practical skill of writing code in a language like Python. Computer science includes programming, but it is broader: it also covers how to represent information (numbers, text, images, sound) inside a machine, how to reason about whether a solution is correct, and how to compare two different solutions to see which one is faster or uses less memory.

At its core, computer science is a problem solving discipline. Suppose you want to find the largest number in a list. There is no single "right" way to do this, but there are better and worse ways, and part of studying computer science is learning to notice the difference. A simple approach: keep track of the largest number seen so far, and walk through the list one item at a time, updating that tracked value whenever you find something bigger. In Python, that idea becomes:

def find_largest(numbers):
    largest = numbers[0]
    for n in numbers:
        if n > largest:
            largest = n
    return largest

Trace through this with the list [3, 7, 2, 9, 4]. largest starts at 3. The loop checks 3 (not greater than 3, no change), then 7 (greater, largest becomes 7), then 2 (no change), then 9 (greater, largest becomes 9), then 4 (no change). The function returns 9, which is indeed the largest value in the list. Notice that the computer did not "understand" the list the way a person would glance at it and immediately see 9. It followed a precise, mechanical procedure, one comparison at a time, and that procedure is guaranteed to work no matter how long the list is.

This example captures the heart of computer science: turning a task a person can describe informally ("find the biggest number") into a precise sequence of steps a machine can execute reliably, every single time. Every concept in this course, from how a computer stores a single character of text to how millions of instructions execute inside a CPU, builds on this same idea. As you move forward, you will learn structured ways of thinking about problems before writing any code at all, which is exactly where the next chapter, computational thinking, begins.
